title: Promise-AM derandomization via targeted hitting sets
formal: Is the following equivalence true? \[\mathrm{prAM}=\mathrm{prNP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{a uniform nondeterministic polynomial-time targeted hitting-set generator exists for co-nondeterministic Boolean circuits.}\] The promise classes and generator are defined below. The generator receives the full description of the circuit it must hit. It must have at least one successful computation branch on every valid circuit, and every successful branch must output a hitting set whenever the circuit accepts at least half of its ordinary inputs. The target permits multiple distinct valid outputs but no input-dependent advice.
why: Derandomization removes the need for public random challenges in efficient proof protocols. A targeted hitting set is a concrete finite object tailored to a verifier. An equivalence would determine whether eliminating randomness necessarily gives such tailored objects in the Arthur–Merlin setting, extending a known structural characterization of ordinary randomized computation.
status_note: The checked Chen–Tell 2023 question and van Melkebeek–Mocelin Sdroievski 2025 journal discussion leave the uniform polynomial-time characterization unresolved. Their partial generator theorem uses different time, advice and length guarantees. Bounded later-work searches through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of this exact equivalence; no exhaustive current-status certification is claimed.

sentences: The question compares promise-Arthur–Merlin derandomization with the existence of targeted hitting sets.
A generator receives a co-nondeterministic circuit and must hit its accepting ordinary inputs whenever they occupy at least half the domain.
Nondeterministic generation must always have a successful branch, and every successful output must satisfy the required hitting guarantee.
The source asks whether eliminating public randomness is equivalent to a uniform polynomial-time generator of this kind.
The checked 2025 journal result establishes a weaker connection involving different time, advice and input-length guarantees.

definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^{*}\); inputs outside \(Y\cup N\) have no correctness requirement. Membership in \(\mathrm{prNP}\) means that there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every \(x\in Y\), some \(u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) satisfies \(V(x,u)=1\), and for every \(x\in N\), every such \(u\) is rejected. Membership in \(\mathrm{prAM}\) means that there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) and a polynomial \(q\) such that Arthur sends a uniformly random \(r\in\{0,1\}^{q(|x|)}\) to Merlin, who sees \(x,r\) and responds with \(u\in\{0,1\}^{q(|x|)}\); for \(x\in Y\), \(\Pr_r[\exists u:W(x,r,u)=1]\ge2/3\), and for \(x\in N\), this probability is at most \(1/3\). Merlin has no computational restriction. Equality means equality of the sets of promise problems recognized in these senses, with a potentially different verifier for each problem. A co-nondeterministic circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit \(C(r,u)\), using constants, fan-in-two AND and OR gates and unary NOT gates, with one output, ordinary input bits \(r\in\{0,1\}^a\), and universally quantified input bits \(u\in\{0,1\}^b\). Its size counts all input and internal gates; put \(m=\max\{2,\operatorname{size}(C)\}\), so \(a,b\le m\). Encode its gates in topological order, with binary predecessor indices and designated ordinary/universal inputs. For \(z\in\{0,1\}^m\), set \(D_C(z)=1\) exactly when \(C(z_1,\ldots,z_a,u)=1\) for every \(u\in\{0,1\}^b\); extra ordinary bits are ignored. Empty universal inputs mean one empty assignment. Define density \(\mu(C)=2^{-m}|\{z:D_C(z)=1\}|\). A targeted generator is one finite nondeterministic Turing machine \(H\), and constants \(K,d\), whose every branch on a valid description \(C\) halts in at most \(K(m+1)^d\) bit steps, either with a distinguished failure symbol or with an explicit nonempty finite list \(S\) of strings in \(\{0,1\}^m\). At least one branch must output a list on every \(C\). If \(\mu(C)\ge1/2\), then every branch that outputs a list must satisfy \(\exists z\in S:D_C(z)=1\). If \(\mu(C)<1/2\), no hitting property is required, but the branch and output-format requirements still apply. All descriptions, nondeterministic choices, list entries and output writes are charged. No random bits, oracle or advice is supplied. The machine can depend on its particular circuit input, not merely on circuit size. Explicit polynomial-length output lists are the table representation of the source’s generators with \(O(\log m)\) seed bits; no compact representation of an exponentially large list is allowed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the equivalence or its logical negation under these definitions. The nontrivial unresolved implication is from promise-AM derandomization to the stated generator; the reverse implication is already established in the cited framework. A positive answer must obtain a single uniform generator with polynomial cost, at least one successful branch for every circuit and no incorrect successful branch on any dense circuit. A generator requiring advice, working only for infinitely many input lengths, using superpolynomial time or handling ordinary deterministic circuits alone does not establish the target. A relativized separation or a counterexample to one proposed generator does not by itself refute the unrelativized equivalence.

context_blocks.text: Chen and Tell’s Open Problem 2.5 restates a question introduced by Goldreich in 2011. It asks for the equivalence with nondeterministically computed targeted hitting-set generators for co-nondeterministic circuits. The input circuit and the treatment of unsuccessful branches are essential parts of that formulation.

The source contrasts this open characterization with the established equivalence between promise-BPP derandomization and deterministic targeted pseudorandom generators. That deterministic-circuit result does not automatically provide the universal-witness circuit guarantee needed here.

The 2025 journal paper of van Melkebeek and Mocelin Sdroievski gives a precise nondeterministic definition: there is a successful branch on every input, and all successful outputs must hit a dense circuit. Its Definitions 3.8 and 3.9 supply the output-list convention used here.

The same journal paper’s Theorem 1.10 derives a targeted generator from a stronger high-time derandomization assumption, with an infinitely-often simulation and nonuniform advice. It is evidence toward the connection but leaves the uniform polynomial-time equivalence unresolved.
